This is the eating disorder where people starve themselves because they are deeply afraid of gaining weight. In many of their families, anorexia showed up across generations. Others had failed treatment again and again.

The gene is called PLIN4. The surprise is where it works: mostly in body fat and muscle, not mainly in the brain.

Researchers at Michigan State University read the parts of each patient's genes that build proteins. This method is called whole-exome sequencing. They checked 32 genes that earlier family studies had flagged. Only one passed strict statistical tests. About 11% of patients carried a rare, likely damaging change in PLIN4. In a large database of people with similar European ancestry, the figure was about 3%. So a patient was nearly four times as likely to carry one.

Families added some evidence. Six patients had a change that probably breaks the gene completely. In four of those six, a relative who also had anorexia carried the very same change. But this small group did not pass the strict test on its own.

So what does PLIN4 do? Inside fat and muscle cells, fat is stored in tiny droplets. PLIN4 makes a protein that coats these droplets. It helps decide how fat is packed away and how it is released for energy. When the gene is broken, cells struggle to store and release fat normally.

How could that lead to an eating disorder? Here the researchers are guessing, and they say so. Faulty fat storage might send false signals of hunger or fullness. It might mix up the hormone messages that fat sends to the brain about the body's energy. Or it might make eating and gaining weight feel physically unpleasant.

The lead researcher, psychiatrist Michael Lutter, compares the finding to BRCA1 and BRCA2. These gene changes raise breast cancer risk in some families. Many genes together shape the risk of anorexia. But a rare change in one key gene may raise that risk a lot in certain families.

This matters because anorexia has one of the highest death rates of any mental illness. Yet the US drug regulator, the FDA, has approved no medicine for it. Treatment is therapy and slowly, carefully getting patients to eat again. Anorexia is also among the least-funded areas at the US National Institutes of Health. Study advisor A.J. Robison links this neglect to an old bias: the belief that anorexia is just vanity in women who want to be thin. The disease is ten times more common in women than in men.

Next, the team will study fat tissue from patients who carry these changes. They want to see how the fat droplets actually look and behave. As Robison puts it, finding a gene will not cure the disease. But it can show what causes it, and that can guide new treatments.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study. The patients were a hand-picked group: severe cases, often with strong family histories, all of European ancestry. They were compared with a public gene database, not with healthy people the team recruited. Most people with anorexia will not carry a PLIN4 change. The researchers say the result must be repeated in larger groups from many ancestries. The idea that a fat-storage problem leads to anorexia has not been tested yet.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Anorexia is usually blamed on the mind alone. For some families, part of it may start in how the body stores fat.

recall.q: Why is the PLIN4 finding surprising, and how strong is the evidence so far?
recall.a: PLIN4 works mainly in body fat and muscle, where it coats fat droplets. It is not mainly a brain gene, so the finding challenges the idea that anorexia lives only in the brain. In this study, 11% of 154 severe patients carried damaging changes, against about 3% in a reference database. But it is a single study of a selected European group, and it needs to be repeated.

cards.title: The US wants to end monkey research. Is neuroscience ready?
cards.body: The US government is moving to end research on monkeys. It wants computer models and lab-grown clumps of cells to take their place. The Transmitter, a neuroscience news site, spoke with more than 40 scientists to ask two questions. Does brain science still need monkeys? And are the replacements ready?

sections.text:
The National Institutes of Health is America's main funder of medical research. Recently it made an unusual offer to one of its national primate research centers. Would the center become an animal sanctuary? That is a place where the monkeys simply live out their lives, with no experiments.

The offer is one sign of a bigger shift. Over the past two years, the US government has taken steps to slowly end animal research. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention closed its primate research program. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said that he and the heads of his department's major agencies are "all deeply committed to ending animal experimentation." He also wants to stop all imports of monkeys for research.

What would replace the animals? The government's answer is a set of tools called new approach methodologies, or NAMs. Some are computer models of how the body works. Others are organoids: tiny clumps of cells grown in a dish that copy part of an organ, such as a small piece of brain.

So brain science must ask whether it still needs nonhuman primates, our closest animal relatives, and whether NAMs can do their job. To find out, the reporters talked to scientists and also read dozens of research papers and government reports.

This piece opens their series, so it gives no verdict yet. Instead, it maps the fight. First, the open questions in neuroscience that scientists say still need primates. Second, the threat to America's network of national primate research centers. Third, monkey models of autism, which the series calls promising but rocky. Fourth, the work to fix key weaknesses in organoids.

The changes have already begun. A primate center in Oregon plans to shrink its monkey colony and move toward non-animal models. And three neuroscientists, Cory Miller, J. Anthony Movshon and Doris Tsao, put their view in the title of an essay: without monkeys, neuroscience has no future.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The policy is moving faster than the science. Monkeys are already leaving the labs, while the tools meant to replace them are still being fixed.

recall.q: What does the US government want to use instead of monkeys in research, and what two questions does this raise for neuroscience?
recall.a: It wants to use new approach methodologies (NAMs), such as computer models and organoids, which are tiny clumps of cells grown in a dish. The two questions are: does neuroscience still need nonhuman primates, and are NAMs ready to replace them?

cards.title: Lincoln's depression, and the man he built through it
cards.body: As a young man, Abraham Lincoln came so close to suicide that his friends kept watch over him. He lived. The darkness kept coming back, and he learned from it. Later he turned his private danger into a warning for a whole nation.

sections.text:
The young man stopped carrying a pocket knife. He did not trust himself with it. His friends in Illinois watched him walk alone in the woods with his gun. They grew so worried that they took turns watching over him. This was Abraham Lincoln in his twenties, long before most people knew his name.

Several things broke at once. He was studying law day and night and had grown dangerously thin. A typhoid epidemic was killing people all around him. It took Ann Rutledge, a young woman who understood his sensitive nature better than almost anyone. People have since invented a whole love story about them, but the real facts are few. What is clear is this: tired and grieving, Lincoln began to think seriously about ending his life.

He lived. But the dark spells came back again and again. Today we would call this depression. The source essay draws on Joshua Wolf Shenk's book Lincoln's Melancholy. It asks a bigger question than how he survived. It asks what the depression made of him, and what he made of it.

At first, he hid it. He became famous for his jokes. In public he was so cheerful that even close colleagues almost never saw him low. But the pain came out as kindness. When a friend fell into depression, Lincoln wrote to him like someone who knew that place from the inside. He wrote that thinking too hard can wear even the sweetest idea thin, until it turns as bitter as death.

At 30, he did something no one discovered for 139 years. He published an unsigned poem in a small Illinois newspaper, printed next to ads for whale oil and cologne. In it, a man walks into a forest to kill himself. The essay sees the poem as Lincoln testing, safely inside his imagination, the lie that suicide tells: that disappearing is the only way to stop the pain.

Three years later, the darkness returned. A few weeks before his 33rd birthday, he wrote to his law partner that he was "the most miserable man living." Then he named the choice plainly. He could not stay as he was, so he must "die or be better." He got better. Depression hides one fact very well: the light can come back.

What he built afterwards carried the mark of what he had lived through. In one of his great speeches, he told Americans that no outside enemy could destroy their country. If it fell, it would fall by its own hand. He had turned his most private danger into a lesson for a nation.

The man who once could not be trusted with a pocket knife went on to teach a whole country what he had learned in those woods. The biggest danger often comes from within. So can the way through.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is an essay, not a study. The idea that depression shaped Lincoln's greatness is how Shenk and the essayist read his life. It is not a proven link. It is also no reason to see suicidal despair as a gift. In Lincoln's worst year, the people around him noticed and kept watch. If you are in that place now, tell someone today.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Depression says the dark will last forever. Lincoln's life is a long record that it does not.

recall.q: In his worst letter, what choice did Lincoln say he faced, and how did his private struggle later show up in his public life?
recall.a: He wrote that he could not stay as he was, so he must die or be better. He got better. Later he told the nation that its real danger came from within: if America fell, it would fall by its own hand.
